newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - ICI, Brit Steel tumble after budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - ICI, Brit Steel tumble after budget.

text.p: Imperial Chemical Industries Plc and other top British industrial groups such as British Steel Plc were the biggest fallers in the UK's FSTE 100 index on Thursday as they fell victim to Wednesday's budget.

A post-budget surge in sterling was seen as depressing the value of their overseas earnings, while the abolition of the dividend tax credit was seen as requiring higher payments into their pension funds.
Analysts said they were considering another round of earnings downgrades as they weighed up the impact of the first budget under a Labour government for 19 years.
BZW, for instance, was said to be considering a 30 million pound ($50.3 million) cut in its 1997 pre-tax profit estimate for ICI to 365 million stg, largely on the dividend effect.
By 1056 GMT, ICI was off 46p, or 5.40 percent, at 802-1/2p and British Steel fell 8-1/4p, or 6.5 percent, to 142p.

Others such as industrial conglomerate BTR Plc, controls maker Seibe Plc, specialist engineer TI Group Plc, building materials group RMC Group Plc and auto parts group GKN Plc also tumbled by as much as six percent.
Chancellor (finance minster) Gordon Brown's budget had set out to boost investment in British industry, yet he failed to deliver the clampdown on consumer spending that some had expected.

Currency markets were quick to draw the conculsion that interest rates would be pushed as much as one percentage point higher in coming months as the newly-independent Bank of England battles to prevent an upturn in consumer spending.

Yet the surge in sterling to a five-year high against the mark, on the back of rising rate expectations, was bad news for companies which derive a large element of their profits from continental Europe and other overseas markets.
For ICI and the rest of the cream of British industry, the budget delivered a further dose of unpleasant medicine because of their large pension liabilities.

Analysts at BZW said nearly half of the FTSE 100 companies' pension funds could become underfunded because of the tax credit abolition, hitting earnings. Industrial companies, with their large workforces and high numbers of pensioners, were seen as most vulnerable.
BZW said the cost of the reduction in the value of company pension funds will reduce average sector earnings by two percent.

"Given that another aspect of this budget is that it looks set to give sterling another push upwards, there must be significant risk that the industrials will come under further pressure over the summer months," it said.
Analysts noted that earnings expectations in a swathe of industrial firms had already been progressively cut in recent months as sterling showed no signs of running out of steam

"It is probably both but I think the real issue has to be sterling," said Peter Cartwright, chemicals analyst at Williams de Broe. "There is going to be another round of earnings downgrades. It will not be as severe as the Christmas round but enough to be noticeable."
Brown's decision to cut the main tax rate on company profits from 33 percent to a record low of 31 percent, provided little comfort against expectations for a hike in interest rates.
Brown said in his budget speech that he shared industry concerns about the strength of sterling and he would address them.
Yet analysts and dealers were not convinced his words would have much impact.

"These overseas earners are mostly out of favour," said the head of equity sales at one top U.S. investment bank. "The $64,000 question is at what point sterling tops out, but at the moment it's hard to see that happening."
